title: Dependency injection and IoC
idea: Dependency injection (DI) means an object receives its collaborators, such as a clock, through its constructor; inversion of control (IoC) moves that wiring decision outside the class.

analogy.text: A camera body does not build its own lens. It has a standard mount, and the photographer attaches a wide or zoom lens for each shoot.
analogy.breaks: A lens swaps mid-shoot; an object usually gets its collaborators once.

points: c03-t06 showed who owns the interface; this page shows how objects receive it.
Time and randomness are hidden dependencies; inject a `Clock` and a seeded `Random`.
Constructor injection keeps fields `final`; setters allow half-built objects that fail later.
A service locator hides dependencies in a global map that leaks between tests.

hero.title: Who decides the clock and the codes

steps.caption: `PassIssuer` lists what it needs in its constructor: a `Clock` and a `CodeSource`. It creates neither.
Asking the clock for now, instead of calling `Instant.now()`, turns time into a dependency someone else picks.
Codes come from a role. A seeded `Random` or a plain sequence both fit the same slot.
In production, `main` passes `Clock.systemUTC()` and `RandomCodes` over a `SecureRandom`.
In a test, the test passes a fixed clock and `Random(42)`, so every run prints the same codes.
Control is inverted: the roots decide the wiring, and `PassIssuer` never changes between them.

code.title: The problem
code.caption: Three ways to hide a dependency: reach for it, set it later, or look it up globally.

walk.text: `new Random()` and `Instant.now()` are buried in the method. No caller can choose either.
So the test can check only that the code has six digits, never which code or expiry.
Setter injection: the field cannot be `final`, and nothing makes a caller call the setter.
The forgotten setter fails at first use, far from where the object was built.
Service locator: the issuer fetches its clock from a static map. Its constructor hides the need.
A clock left over from an earlier test leaks in: the pass expires in 2020.

code.title: The fix
code.caption: Constructor injection of time and randomness. The test picks a fixed clock and a seeded generator.

walk.text: `CodeSource` makes randomness a role. `PassIssuer` compiles without knowing which generator runs.
`RandomCodes` wraps any `Random`, including `SecureRandom`. `SequenceCodes` is an id generator for readable tests.
Constructor injection: `final` fields, null rejected at once, so the object is complete.
`clock.instant()` asks the injected clock. Expiry is now exactly predictable.
The test is its own composition root. `Random(42)` gives the same codes on every run.
A missing dependency fails at construction with its name, not later inside `issue`.

pitfalls: Calling `Instant.now()` or `new Random()` inside logic leaves tests checking shapes, never values.
Field injection hides dependencies and blocks `final`; tests then need reflection to set fields.
A constructor with seven parameters signals an SRP problem; split the class instead of hiding them.

quiz.q: Why does the fixed test print the same two codes on every run?
options: `Random` caches its last value between runs
`new Random(42)` always yields the same sequence
The JVM reuses codes for the same guest
quiz.why: A `Random` built with a seed replays one fixed sequence. Injecting it lets the test choose that seed; production injects `SecureRandom` instead.

takeaway: Ask for collaborators in the constructor; let the composition root choose them.

starters: What is the difference between DI and the Dependency Inversion Principle?
